---
title: "Bayes at the Edge"
abstract: |
  Accuracy-first epistemology defends Bayesian conditionalization by showing that, among rules that respond only to what one learns, it does best by the lights of accuracy. Externalists who think inexact knowledge needs a margin for error face a problem. Such agents can learn something without learning that it is what they learned, and then other rules do better. Meehan and Zhang argue that conditionalization can be restored. Among rules whose output depends only on the prior and on what is learned, it has the highest expected accuracy summed over every possible way of learning. I argue that this fails for the agents who motivate it. If every way an agent has of learning about a magnitude leaves a margin for error around the truth, then the truth is never at the edge of what she learns. Conditionalization is then accuracy-dominated by a rule that responds only to what she learns. Meehan and Zhang's sum escapes this result because it counts, with equal weight, learning in which the truth does sit at the edge. Statisticians call this condition coarsening at random, and margins forbid it. The upshot is a dilemma for externalists. They can conditionalize on what they know without an accuracy vindication, or they can update on signals they can track, giving up margins around the truth.
bibliography: bayes-at-the-edge.bib
---

# The problem {#sec-intro}

Bayesian conditionalization says that when one learns *p*, and nothing stronger, one should adopt one's prior conditional on *p*. Its best-known defence is accuracy-theoretic. @GreavesWallace2006 showed that if the propositions one might learn form a partition, then among plans that respond only to what one learns, conditionalizing has the highest expected accuracy. @BriggsPettigrew2020 turned this into a dominance argument [corrected by @Nielsen2021]. Both results presuppose that whenever one learns *p*, one is in a position to tell that *p* is what one learned.

Externalists deny this. On @Williamson2000's view, inexact knowledge requires a margin for error. Suppose the hand of an unmarked clock points at 17 and you cannot discriminate neighbouring positions. Then the most you know by looking is that it points somewhere from 16 to 18. Had it pointed at 18, you would have known only that it pointed somewhere from 17 to 19. Since 18 is compatible with what you know, you do not know that 16-to-18 is what you know.

When learning is opaque in this way, the accuracy arguments turn against conditionalization. Among plans that respond only to what is learned, the one with highest expected accuracy conditionalizes on the proposition that one has learned *p*, not on *p* itself [@Schoenfield2017]. On the clock, that plan makes one certain of the hand's exact position. An externalist who wants to be a Bayesian, and to connect rationality with accuracy, seems to be stuck [@Schultheis2025].

@MeehanZhang2025 offer a way out. They require that the credence a rule recommends depend only on the prior and on the proposition learned, not on the learning situation that produced it. They call this *global evidential constancy*. They then evaluate rules not by expected accuracy in the agent's actual situation but by *total* expected accuracy: the sum of expected accuracies over every learning situation compatible with the prior. Their main result (Fact 10, p. 330) is that, among globally evidentially constant rules, conditionalization uniquely maximizes total expected accuracy. Bayes is back.

I argue that Bayes is back only for learners who lack the feature that made the problem. The central claim is a dominance result. Suppose every way an agent has of learning about a magnitude leaves a margin for error around the truth, as Williamson's clock and Meehan and Zhang's own examples do. Then whatever she learns, the truth lies in its interior, never next to a possibility it excludes. In that case some globally evidentially constant rule is at least as accurate as conditionalization at every combination of learning situation and state that is possible for her. It is strictly more accurate whenever what she learns has an edge (@sec-dominance).

Informally: knowing that you cannot tell neighbouring cases apart is information about where, within what you know, the truth lies. Conditionalization throws that information away and pays for it at every possibility you leave open.

Meehan and Zhang's sum comes out in conditionalization's favour because their measure is an instance of what statisticians call *coarsening at random*. For each proposition, it puts the same weight on learning that proposition at every state where it is true, including states at its edge (@sec-edge). Margins around the truth forbid exactly this. I take up Meehan and Zhang's best replies in @sec-whose. In @sec-recommend I ask what accuracy does recommend for such agents, and find that it recommends credences that the theory of knowledge which produced the margins says they cannot have. The conclusion is a dilemma (@sec-conclusion). The externalist can conditionalize on what she knows and give up the accuracy vindication. Or she can keep the accuracy vindication and give up margins around the truth, updating instead on signals she can track.[^antecedents]

[^antecedents]: Some pieces have antecedents.
    - Kenny Easwaran observed, in a comment on @Pettigrew2025, that Meehan and Zhang's total amounts to expected accuracy when each learning situation is equally likely [@Easwaran2025].
    - Likelihood-weighted rules that maximize expected accuracy under uncertainty about how one learns are in @Gallow2021, @IsaacsRussell2023 and @EaswaranNielsen2025.
    - @Salow2018 contrasts evidence centred on the truth with evidence centred on a best guess, in the course of arguing that the former allows inquiries biased in one's favour.
    - @Dorst2020 gives a dominance argument against certain clock models, concerning credence in a single proposition.

    What is new here:
    - a dominance result that holds across every learning situation with margins around the truth, witnessed by a globally evidentially constant rule;
    - the diagnosis of how evaluations that vindicate conditionalization escape it;
    - the argument of @sec-recommend.

# Margins around the truth {#sec-margins}

I use Meehan and Zhang's framework.
- A *prior space* is a finite set of states *S* with a regular prior π.
- A *learning situation* is a function *E* taking each state *s* to the strongest proposition *E*(*s*) one learns there. Learning is factive, so *s* ∈ *E*(*s*).
- An *updating rule* takes a prior space and a learning situation and returns, for each state, the credence to adopt there.
- A rule is *globally evidentially constant* if the credence it recommends at *s* depends only on (*S*, π) and *E*(*s*). Equivalently (their Fact 5, p. 316), it is a function from propositions to credences, *f*(*p*). Conditionalization, *b*(*p*) = π(· | *p*), is one such rule.

Margins come from measurement. Suppose an instrument, or an eye, reports a value *a* when the true value is *v*. The most one can know is a region around *a*, but how large a region? Two answers are found in the literature.
- On the first, which @Williamson2013 offers and @Weatherson2013 defends, the strongest thing one knows after a reading *a* with error *e* = |*a* − *v*| is that the value lies within *e* + *m* of *a*. Here *m* > 0 is the margin needed for safety. Since *v* is within *e* of *a*, every value within *m* of *v* is within *e* + *m* of *a*. The region is centred on the appearance, but it always leaves a margin of *m* around the truth.
- On the second, associated with @Stalnaker2009, @CohenComesana2013 and @Salow2018, what one learns is centred on a best guess. For Salow, talk of margins for error is talk of "the maximum distance between my best guess and the actual hand", and the truth can lie anywhere within that distance of the guess, including at its edge.

The difference is whether there is slack: a margin around the truth over and above the error.

The argument concerns the first kind of view, and it is the view that generates the opacity Meehan and Zhang address. Their illustration is Olivia, who "knows that, if the butter weighs *x* oz., then she will learn by weighing it in her hand that it weighs (*x* ± 1) oz., but nothing more precise" (p. 294). They describe the case as "a variant of the austere clock from Williamson" (p. 294, n. 6). They also cite Williamson's own gloss: what one learns can depend on facts of one's environment "without themselves entailing those facts" (p. 294).

To put this in their framework, think of the states as the possible values of a magnitude, ordered on a line or round a circle at increments no larger than the margin. Two states are *neighbours* if they are adjacent. Williamson's margin principle, with what one learns identified with what one comes to know, says that the strongest proposition learned at *s* contains *s*'s neighbours. Meehan and Zhang mention the identification as "one influential externalist view of evidence" (p. 290, n. 4). Call a learning situation *two-sided* if, for every state *s*, *E*(*s*) contains *s* and its neighbours. Margins may be wider than one step and may vary from state to state; only the immediate neighbours matter here.

For a proposition *p*, let its *interior* be the set of states of *p* whose neighbours all lie in *p*. Let its *rim* be the rest of *p*: the states that sit next to a state *p* excludes. Then:

**Observation.** If *E* is two-sided and *E*(*s*) = *p*, then *s* is in the interior of *p*.

For if *s* were on the rim, a neighbour of *s* would lie outside *p*, whereas a two-sided *E*(*s*) contains all of *s*'s neighbours. @Williamson2014 [p. 980] proves the special case for his clock, where what is known at *w* is the interval of width 2*h*+1 centred on *w*: "R(w) is known only at w". So Olivia learns that the butter weighs from 16 to 18 oz. only if it weighs 17. Dana, who weighs butter of 15, 16 or 17 oz. with her right hand and whose prior is (0.2, 0.6, 0.2) (p. 300), learns {15, 16} only at 15.

One caveat concerns scale. The margin must have positive width relative to the prior. If the grid is refined while the margin stays one step wide, the rim's probability shrinks toward zero, and so does everything that follows. Williamson's margins are fixed in physical units, so refining the grid widens them in steps.

# Conditionalization is dominated {#sec-dominance}

An accuracy measure assigns a score *A*(*c*, *s*) to credence function *c* at state *s*. The two standard examples are these:
- The logarithmic score is ln *c*(*s*).
- The Brier score is minus the sum, over propositions, of the squared distance between one's credence in a proposition and its truth value.

Meehan and Zhang use the Brier score and an additive logarithmic score of the same propositionwise form (p. 302).

**Proposition.** Let *A* be the logarithmic score, or any additive, continuous, strictly proper score in the sense of @Predd2009, and let π be regular. Then there is a globally evidentially constant rule *f*~*A*~ such that, for every two-sided learning situation *E* and every state *s*,

> *A*(*f*~*A*~(*E*(*s*)), *s*) ≥ *A*(π(· | *E*(*s*)), *s*),

with strict inequality whenever *E*(*s*) has a nonempty rim. On a connected scale this means whenever anything short of the whole space is learned.

*Proof.* Let *p* be a proposition with a nonempty interior and a nonempty rim, and let *c* = π(· | *p*). Let *K* be the set of credence functions concentrated on the interior of *p*. Define *f*~*A*~(*p*) as the projection of *c* onto *K* in the divergence that *A* determines. For any other proposition, let *f*~*A*~(*p*) = *c*. A two-sided learner never learns a proposition with an empty interior.

By the Observation, if *E*(*s*) = *p* then *s* is in the interior of *p*, so the credence function certain of *s* lies in *K*. Two cases:
- **Logarithmic score.** The projection is π(· | int *p*). For *s* in the interior, π(*s* | int *p*) = π(*s*)/π(int *p*) > π(*s*)/π(*p*) = π(*s* | *p*), since regularity gives the rim positive probability.
- **Additive scores.** @Predd2009 show that such a score differs from minus a Bregman divergence between *c* and the truth-value assignment only by a term that depends on the state alone (their eq. 5). Their Proposition 3 gives, for the projection *q* of *c* onto a closed convex set and any point *y* of that set, *d*(*y*, *q*) ≤ *d*(*y*, *c*) − *d*(*q*, *c*). Take *y* to be the truth-value assignment at an interior state *s*. Since *c* gives the rim positive probability, *c* ∉ *K*, so *d*(*q*, *c*) > 0 and *q* is strictly more accurate than *c* at *s*.

For the Brier score the projection is Euclidean: it adds the rim's probability equally to each interior state. ∎[^unbounded]

[^unbounded]: Predd et al.'s Proposition 3 is stated for divergences with bounded gradient. Unbounded scores, such as the additive logarithmic score, need the more careful argument of their unbounded case. Here it is simplified by the fact that propositions which do not cut across *p* get the same credence from every function concentrated on *p*. I have also checked numerically, on lines of four and five states with random priors, that the projection dominates under the additive log score and under the spherical score.

Five remarks.

1. **Global evidential constancy.** The rules respond only to what is learned, so they satisfy evidential constancy and non-contrastiveness, and hence the idempotence Meehan and Zhang defend (Fact 6, p. 320). Followability does not separate them from conditionalization either. As Meehan and Zhang point out, conditionalization is no more "luminous" than its rivals in opaque problems (p. 306). A rule that tells you to conditionalize on what you learned asks no less of your capacity to tell what you learned than a rule that tells you to discount its rim.

2. **Dependence on the score.** The dominating rule depends on the score, as Joyce's dominating credences do [@Joyce1998]. π(· | int *p*) is not in general Brier-dominant. With two or more interior states, no one rule dominates conditionalization under every score. That conditionalization is dominated does not depend on the score.

3. **The examples.**
   - Suppose Olivia's prior is uniform. When the butter weighs 17 she learns [16, 18], and conditionalization gives each weight credence 1/3. The dominating rules make her certain of 17, and she is right, since [16, 18] is learned only at 17.
   - At 15, Dana's conditionalized credence (0.25, 0.75, 0) has Brier score −2.25. That is worse than the −2.08 of keeping her prior (p. 302, Table 1; this is their Fact 3). The dominating rule scores 0.

4. **Uniformity.** Meehan and Zhang show that for any globally evidentially constant rule there are problems in which another such rule does better: "There is no rule that rules them all" (p. 327). Their Fact 7 (p. 324) says that no such rule does at least as well as conditionalization in every updating problem. The proof uses, for each *p*, the transparent problem of learning whether *p*. There *p* is learned at every state where it is true, rim included. Restrict attention to two-sided problems and the situation reverses: a single rule does at least as well as conditionalization in every one of them. It follows that conditionalization is suboptimal under every weighting of two-sided learning situations that gives some weight to learning a proposition with a rim, whatever the weights are taken to mean.

5. **Relation to existing dominance arguments.** The result inverts @BriggsPettigrew2020: for partitional learning, every rule other than conditionalization is dominated; for two-sided learning, conditionalization is. It differs from three nearby results:
   - @Dorst2020's argument against "effacing" clock models concerns credence in a single proposition.
   - @Das2022's exploitability results concern betting.
   - @Schoenfield2017's meta-conditionalization responds to the learning situation and not only to what is learned.

## Graded margins

Real discrimination is graded. Psychometric functions slope, and the threshold for "cannot tell apart" is set by a choice of performance level. Suppose learning is stochastic, so that occasionally the truth falls on the rim of what is learned. Then pointwise dominance fails: a rule that is certain of the interior is infinitely wrong under the log score in the rare cases where the truth is on the rim.

What remains is a comparison of expected accuracy. By Meehan and Zhang's own Lemma 1 (p. 344), the globally evidentially constant rule with the highest expected accuracy assigns each state of *p* credence proportional to π(*s*)λ~*p*~(*s*). Here λ~*p*~(*s*) is the probability of learning *p* at *s*. Conditionalization is optimal only if λ~*p*~ is flat across *p*. When the probability of learning *p* falls off toward its edge, as graded margins make it, the optimal rule raises the centre and lowers the rim. This is the update that @EaswaranNielsen2025 [p. 1129] derive for an unmarked dial with a "cosine" error density. So the graded case changes the form of the verdict, from dominance to expected inferiority, but not its direction.

# How Bayes comes back {#sec-edge}

Why, then, does Meehan and Zhang's total favour conditionalization? Their generalization of it is instructive. Let λ weight learning situations, and let λ~*p*~(*s*) be the total weight of situations in which *p* is learned at *s*. Read λ as a probability of being in each situation. Then their Lemma 1 says that the best rule conditionalizes on the fact that *p* was learned, with λ~*p*~(*s*) as the likelihood. This is Easwaran's observation: the total is "basically equivalent to assuming you are equally likely to be using it in any of these situations" [@Easwaran2025]. Conditionalization on *p* itself comes out best iff λ~*p*~(*s*) is the same at every state of *p*. This is Meehan and Zhang's *extensionality* (Fact 11, p. 337; Lemma 2, p. 345).

Statisticians call the condition *coarsening at random*: data are coarsened at random when the probability of observing a set is the same at every point of the set [@HeitjanRubin1991]. @Gill1997 showed that under this condition, and only under it, conditioning on the observed set gives the same answer as conditioning on the fact that it was observed. @GrunwaldHalpern2003 [Theorem 3.1] restate the result for updating. As @GillGrunwald2008 [p. 2410] put it, the condition "precisely characterizes when one can ignore the distinction between the fact that an event has been observed, and the fact that an event has happened". The Monty Hall problem is the standard illustration. Meehan and Zhang note this in discussing Pearl's lesson that "we must also consider what information could have been reported" (p. 311, n. 21). Their extensionality is coarsening at random, and their Fact 11 is an instance of the statistical characterization.

Their own measure weights every factive learning situation equally, and so it is coarsened at random. In Easwaran's gloss, which proposition one learns is "chosen uniformly at random from the set of all propositions true at the world" [@Easwaran2025]. So the total credits each proposition as if it were learned equally often at each of its states, including the states on its rim.[^perm]

[^perm]: Any weighting unchanged by permutations of the states is extensional. If *s* and *s*′ both lie in *p*, the transposition of *s* and *s*′ maps the situations that deliver *p* at *s* one-to-one onto those that deliver *p* at *s*′, preserving weight. The counting measure is permutation-invariant because it treats *S* as an unstructured set. Margins are defined by adjacency, and a weighting that respects adjacency need not be permutation-invariant.

For a two-sided learner, extensionality is impossible, not merely contestable, as Meehan and Zhang allow when they call it "bedrock" (p. 337). The argument has three steps:
1. Extensionality requires the weight on learning *p* to be the same at every state of *p*.
2. By the Observation, a two-sided situation delivers *p* only at states in *p*'s interior. So a weighting confined to two-sided situations puts zero weight on learning *p* at its rim.
3. So such a weighting is extensional only if no proposition with a rim gets positive weight. On a connected scale, that means nothing is learned but the whole space.

In the statistical idiom, margins around the truth guarantee that coarsening is not at random. That holds for every weighting of two-sided situations under which something nontrivial is learned.

Coarsening at random can be restored with mixtures, but only by adding learning that is exact at an edge. On Dana's scale, mix her right-hand situation with gauges that err in one direction only. Weight the following situations 2/7, 1/7, 1/7, 1/7 and 2/7, where each triple gives what is learned at 15, 16 and 17:

| Weight | At 15 | At 16 | At 17 | Notes |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---|
| 2/7 | {15} | *S* | *S* | |
| 1/7 | {15, 16} | *S* | {16, 17} | Dana's right hand |
| 1/7 | *S* | {15, 16} | {16, 17} | |
| 1/7 | *S* | *S* | {17} | |
| 2/7 | *S* | {16, 17} | *S* | |

Then {15, 16} has weight 1/7 at each of its states, {16, 17} has 2/7 at each, and *S* has 4/7 at each. The mixture is coarsened at random, and conditionalization is again optimal. The work is done by situations that deliver {15, 16} at 16 or {16, 17} at 16. These are gauges with no margin on the side facing the excluded possibility, which a two-sided learner never is. Even then the proportions must be exactly right. @GrunwaldHalpern2003 [§4] show more generally that, for overlapping observations, coarsening at random holds only in special cases.

The same pattern runs through models in which conditionalization has seemed accuracy-friendly despite opacity:
- @Carr2021's clock spreads prior credence evenly over world–evidence pairs.
- Isaacs and Russell's clock lets the guess fall equally often one step either side of the truth.
- @EaswaranNielsen2025 [p. 1120] note that their dial with uniform error is conditionalization-friendly because "for every signal, every world that gives it a non-zero probability gives it the same probability".

In each case the truth is as likely to be at the edge of what is conditioned on as in its middle, which is to say there is no slack. Coarsening at random also suffices for the other good properties of conditionalization: the expected posterior equals the prior, and expected accuracy is at least that of not updating [@Good1967]. So the predictable biases of conditionalization on opaque evidence that @Salow2018, @AhmedSalow2019 and @Das2023 describe all require that it fail. They do not follow from its failure, though. Williamson's symmetric clock is not coarsened at random, yet conditionalizing there is unbiased.

# Whose accuracy? {#sec-whose}

Meehan and Zhang anticipate the obvious complaint. "By stipulation, Dana knows her learning situation", and other rules do better in it, so why should she care how conditionalization fares elsewhere (p. 333)? They reply in two parts:
- If the complaint is really about global evidential constancy, they reply that scepticism about it is scepticism about conditionalization itself (p. 334).
- If it is about weighting learning situations equally, then extensionality is bedrock (p. 337).

They add that a "low-level" rationality, sensitive to "individual psychological dispositions and environmental conditions", may diverge from "high-level" Bayesian rationality (p. 338). The Proposition puts pressure on each part.

*Evidential constancy.* The dominating rules are globally evidentially constant, so the complaint is not about evidential constancy in Meehan and Zhang's formal sense. But they also motivate the constraint with a slogan, "same prior over *S*, same evidence about *S*, same posterior over *S*" (p. 309). Read across agents, the slogan says that two agents with the same prior who learn the same proposition should end in the same place, whatever they know about how they learned it. A right-handed Dana who knows her learning is two-sided, and a Dana who knows she will use her more sensitive left hand, which "can tell … whether or not it weighs 17 oz." (p. 320), share a prior. Both can learn {15, 16}. The Proposition gives the first a reason to adopt a rule the second has reason to avoid.

That is a breach of the slogan, but it is the right breach. The cross-agent slogan says that what one could have learned instead is irrelevant to what one should believe on learning *p*: "neither here nor there", as they put it (p. 319). That is the coarsening-at-random assumption in normative form, and Monty Hall is the standard counterexample to it. Meehan and Zhang grant that in opaque versions of Monty Hall "it is less obvious that the standard solution still applies" (p. 311, n. 21). The present cases are opaque Monty Halls. What Dana could have learned at 16 is part of why learning {15, 16} tells her she is at 15.

The slogan's within-agent core, idempotence, is untouched. Consider a Dana who uses both hands, left at *t*~1~ and right at *t*~2~ (p. 321). She does not know that all her learning is two-sided, so the Proposition does not apply to her. If her rule is the one that maximizes expected accuracy over her uncertainty about which hand delivers what, it is a single globally evidentially constant rule, and so idempotent by Fact 6. It is not conditionalization, unless the weights she gives the two hands happen to be coarsened at random.

*Weights.* The Proposition makes weights idle for the agents in question. Dominance compares options across the agent's epistemic possibilities [@Joyce1998; @Pettigrew2016]. If those possibilities include only two-sided ways of learning, conditionalization loses at every one of them under every weighting. To restore it, the evaluation must include learning the agent knows she is not doing. Meehan and Zhang's rule-consequentialist analogy ("do not jaywalk", p. 289) suggests how this might be defended: put the chooser of a rule behind a veil. That yields a dilemma.
- A veil over *persons*, behind which one is equally likely to be any learner who shares the prior, weights learning situations by how often they occur. Two-sided learning then gets real weight, and the result is not conditionalization.
- A veil over *situations*, behind which every factive situation is equally likely, yields Meehan and Zhang's counting measure and hence conditionalization. But its weights express indifference to the structure of the scale, and its chooser must be ignorant of how she learns, which Dana is stipulated not to be.

Pettigrew's gloss is apt. The result shows that "the negative expected effects of being exposed to certain evidence functions and conditionalizing on them are counterbalanced by the positive expected effects of doing this when exposed to other evidence functions". He adds that it "relies on you thinking each evidence function is equally likely" [@Pettigrew2025]. For a two-sided learner, the counterbalancing is done by learners at the edge.

*Uncertain margins.* An agent may be uncertain how she learns. If she is certain only that her learning is two-sided, with margins of unknown and varying width, the Proposition still applies, since it uses nothing more. If she gives some credence to learning that is exact at an edge, dominance fails and the comparison is one of expected accuracy. Then Lemma 1 applies, and conditionalization is optimal only if her credences happen to be coarsened at random. Unlike the counting measure, credences tied to the actual structure of her learning have no reason to be.

*Two levels.* If Bayesianism is the theory of high-level rationality, then the high level is the rationality of learners without margins around the truth. It is not the rationality of Olivia, of right-handed Dana, or of the clock-watcher, the cases used on p. 294 to motivate the problem. Meehan and Zhang write that "one does not have to be an internalist to subscribe to extensionality; the principle is compatible with evidence externalism as well" (p. 338). That is true of externalism in general. It is not true of the margin-based externalism their examples rely on.

# What accuracy recommends {#sec-recommend}

If conditionalization is dominated, what does accuracy recommend instead? Over two-sided learning, dominance favours rules that give the rim no credence at all. Any rule that gives the rim positive credence, including conservative mixtures of the dominating rule and conditionalization, is dominated in turn by its own projection onto the interior. If the agent knows exactly how she learns, the verdict is stronger still: for Olivia, who learns each proposition at only one state, the only undominated response is certainty of that state. That is Schoenfield's meta-conditionalization, now as a dominance verdict. And it is the verdict Meehan and Zhang's framework was built to block.

For an externalist who identifies evidence with knowledge, these recommendations are not just surprising; they cannot be followed. Suppose Olivia, at 17, becomes certain that the butter weighs 17 because she has learned [16, 18]. Her certainty is true. It is also safe, since she would form it only where it is true: [16, 18] is learned only at 17. Nothing in Williamson's account of knowledge seems to deny it the status of knowledge. But then the strongest thing she knows is that the butter weighs 17, and her learning was not two-sided after all. A two-sided knower cannot follow the dominating rules and remain two-sided.

Suppose, then, that we restrict attention to stable rules, which never make her certain of more than she knows. Concavity then gives a further result: for every ε between 0 and 1, the mixture (1 − ε)*f* + ε*b* scores at least (1 − ε)*A*(*f*) + ε*A*(*b*) at every state. So it is strictly more accurate than conditionalization wherever *f* is, while giving every state of *p* positive credence. This is the technique of Meehan and Zhang's Fact 4 (p. 304). With ε large enough, such a mixture produces no high credence in anything stronger than what she knows, on any threshold for belief short of certainty. So even among stable rules, conditionalization is dominated. What singles it out is not accuracy but a separate demand: that credence be the prior conditioned on what one knows.[^ho]

[^ho]: Higher-order principles do not change the picture. On Williamson's margin-one clock, conditionalization produces Dorst's "effacing" evidence about whether the hand is at an even position [@Dorst2020]. The pure dominating rule, which there coincides with meta-conditionalization, does not. The conservative mixtures avoid effacing evidence but fail positive access: at 17 with ε = 0.3 one is certain of [16, 18] yet only 0.8 confident that she should be certain of it. With margins two steps wide and the immediate-neighbour interior, every rule in the family effaces some proposition. Dorst takes such results as reasons to reject the models, which is the second option of the dilemma below.

So for an accuracy-first externalist, margins around the truth are unstable. Accuracy pushes her toward credences that outrun her knowledge in just the way her theory of knowledge forbids, and the only thing that stops the push is a norm that is not about accuracy.

# Conclusion: a dilemma {#sec-conclusion}

The externalist Bayesian wanted three things:
- conditionalization on what one learns;
- the opacity that margins around the truth produce;
- an explanation of conditionalization's rationality in terms of accuracy.

She can have only two of them.

One option keeps conditionalization on what one knows, margins and all, and gives up the accuracy explanation. Rational credence is then evidential probability, the prior conditioned on one's knowledge, taken as a basic norm [@Williamson2000; @Das2022]. This is the first of the externalist responses Meehan and Zhang describe and hoped to improve on (p. 288). For Williamson, accuracy considerations were never the ground of the norm, so little is lost. For accuracy-first epistemology, a great deal is: its explanation of conditionalization stops at exactly the agents externalism is about.

The other option keeps accuracy and gives up margins around the truth. The agent updates on a signal she can track, such as a best guess or an appearance, without slack [@Stalnaker2009; @CohenComesana2013; @Salow2018]. If the signal goes into the state space, learning it is partitional. Conditionalizing on it is then vindicated by the original arguments, and the resulting credences about the world are proportional to prior times likelihood, as in @Gallow2021, @IsaacsRussell2023 and @EaswaranNielsen2025. Conditionalization survives as updating on what one responds to, not on what one knows. Salow notes that the best-guess model has its critics and that defending it is "a promissory note" [@Salow2018, n. 31]; this option inherits that debt.

Meehan and Zhang's theorem is correct, and it shows something real. Averaged over every way of learning, the selection effects that hurt conditionalization cancel. But they cancel because the average includes learners who can learn a proposition at its edge. For learners whose knowledge always leaves a margin around the truth, nothing cancels. Bayes is back only where the truth can sit at the edge of what one knows.
